title: Do penguin species differ in flipper length?
text:
Code: read the data and compute the numbers
library(tidyverse)

penguins <- read_csv("../data/example/penguins.csv", show_col_types = FALSE)

# Mean flipper length per species (2 penguins have no measurement)
flipper_means <- penguins %>%
  filter(!is.na(flipper_length_mm)) %>%
  group_by(species) %>%
  summarise(mean_mm = mean(flipper_length_mm))

mean_of <- function(sp) flipper_means %>% filter(species == sp) %>% pull(mean_mm)
gentoo_vs_chinstrap_mm <- mean_of("Gentoo") - mean_of("Chinstrap")
gentoo_vs_adelie_mm <- mean_of("Gentoo") - mean_of("Adelie")

n_penguins <- nrow(penguins)
n_islands <- n_distinct(penguins$island)
n_no_flipper <- sum(is.na(penguins$flipper_length_mm))
first_year <- min(penguins$year)
last_year <- max(penguins$year)




Code: make the figure
set.seed(3901)  # same jitter on every render
penguins %>%
  filter(!is.na(flipper_length_mm)) %>%
  ggplot(aes(x = species, y = flipper_length_mm, color = species)) +
  geom_boxplot(outlier.shape = NA, width = 0.5) +
  geom_jitter(width = 0.15, alpha = 0.5, size = 1.5) +
  scale_color_viridis_d(end = 0.7) +
  labs(
    title = "Gentoo penguins have the longest flippers",
    x = "Species",
    y = "Flipper length (mm)"
  ) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 14) +
  theme(legend.position = "none")








Figure 1: Flipper length by species. Each point is one penguin; each box shows the middle half of a species, and the line inside it is the median.





Finding. Gentoo penguins have the longest flippers, on average about 21 mm longer than Chinstrap and 27 mm longer than Adelie penguins.
Limitation. These are 344 penguins measured on 3 islands near Palmer Station, Antarctica, in 2007–2009; 2 have no flipper measurement.
Data source. Horst, A. M., Hill, A. P., & Gorman, K. B. (2020). palmerpenguins: Palmer Archipelago (Antarctica) penguin data (R package). https://allisonhorst.github.io/palmerpenguins/ License: CC0.

title: Guided Project: Statistical Transformations and Coordinate Systems
text:
Part A · Fairness
My group: is sex My outcome: is income greater than $50,000 (income == “>50K”).
Question A: Of each sex (group), what share has more than $50,000? Question B: Of everyone earning more than $50,000, what share is each female and what share is male?

A0 · My group and my outcome

a_data <- fairness %>%
  mutate(
    group = sex,
    has_outcome = income == ">50K"
  )

a_data %>%
  count(group, has_outcome) %>%
  print(n = Inf)

# A tibble: 4 × 3
  group  has_outcome     n
  <chr>  <lgl>       <int>
1 Female FALSE        1477
2 Female TRUE          180
3 Male   FALSE        2328
4 Male   TRUE         1015




A1 · The rate within each group (question A)

a1 <- ggplot(a_data, aes(y = group, fill = has_outcome)) +
  geom_bar(position = "fill") +
  labs(x = "Share of the group", y = NULL, fill = "Income >50K")

show_plot(a1)







Figure 1: Share of each group with the outcome.





The plot shows that men have a higher rate of earning more than $50,000 (30.4%) compared to women (10.9%). Each bar represents 100% of its respective sex group, allowing me to compare the income proportions even though the groups have different numbers of people.


A2 · Rates with their standard error

a2_rates <- a_data %>%
  drop_na(has_outcome) %>%
  group_by(group) %>%
  summarize(
    n = n(),
    rate = mean(has_outcome),
    se = sqrt(rate * (1 - rate) / n)
  )

a2_rates

# A tibble: 2 × 4
  group      n  rate      se
  <chr>  <int> <dbl>   <dbl>
1 Female  1657 0.109 0.00764
2 Male    3343 0.304 0.00795

a2 <- ggplot(a2_rates,
             aes(x = rate, y = group,
                 xmin = rate - se,
                 xmax = rate + se)) +
  geom_pointrange() +
  # Many groups, and the labels touch the points? Keep every group, and use
  # vjust = -0.8, size = 3 instead of nudge_y = 0.3.
  geom_text(aes(label = paste("n =", n)), nudge_y = 0.3) +
  labs(x = "Rate (share of the group with the outcome)", y = NULL)

show_plot(a2)







Figure 2: Rate in each group, with ± one standard error and the group size.





The male group has a slightly wider standard error range (0.00795) than the female group (0.00764), although the difference is very small. Both groups have relatively large sample sizes, so their estimated rates have fairly small standard errors. The plot keeps both groups visible rather than dropping either one.


A3 · Zoom or filter?

a3_table <- a_data %>%
  count(group) %>%
  arrange(desc(n))
a3_table

# A tibble: 2 × 2
  group      n
  <chr>  <int>
1 Male    3343
2 Female  1657

a3_start <- 800

a3_counts <- ggplot(a_data, aes(y = group)) +
  geom_bar() +
  labs(x = "Count", y = NULL)

a3_zoom <- a3_counts +
  coord_cartesian(xlim = c(a3_start, max(a3_table$n)), expand = FALSE)

# A warning about removed rows here is expected (Session 2, slide 5).
a3_filter <- a3_counts +
  scale_x_continuous(limits = c(a3_start, max(a3_table$n)))

# Lie Factor (Tufte, 2001, p. 57) of the zoomed plot, largest vs smallest
# group: how many times the picture exaggerates the difference.
a3_largest <- max(a3_table$n)
a3_smallest <- min(a3_table$n)
a3_lie_factor <-
  ((a3_largest - a3_start) / (a3_smallest - a3_start)) /
  (a3_largest / a3_smallest)
a3_lie_factor

[1] 1.470793

show_plot(a3_counts)
show_plot(a3_zoom)
show_plot(a3_filter)











(a) From 0











(b) Zoomed











(c) Filtered







Figure 3: Counts per group: from 0, zoomed and filtered.




The zoomed plot’s Lie Factor (largest vs smallest group) is 1.47.
The original plot shows the full counts of men and women starting from zero. The zoomed plot starts at 800 which makes the difference between the groups appear larger. Its Lie Factor is approximately 1.47, meaning the visual difference is exaggerated by about 1.47 times. The filtered plot removes the bars because their starting point of zero falls outside the selected axis limits. I would publish the original plot because it shows the full counts without exaggerating the difference.


A4 · Each group’s share of everyone with the outcome (question B)

a4_shares <- a_data %>%
  filter(has_outcome) %>%
  count(group) %>%
  mutate(share = n / sum(n))

a4 <- ggplot(a4_shares, aes(x = share, y = group)) +
  geom_col() +
  labs(x = "Share of everyone with the outcome", y = NULL)

show_plot(a4)







Figure 4: Each group’s share of everyone with the outcome.





A1 and A2 show that men have a higher income rate (30.4%) than women (10.9%). A4 also points in the same direction because men make up 84.9% of everyone earning above $50,000, compared to 15.1% for women. My original Module 11 question requires Question A because I want to compare the proportion earning above $50,000 within each sex group, rather than the share of all high-income earners.

Part B · Sports
My group, outcome and value: My group is surface, my outcome is matches lasting more than 120 minutes (minutes > 120), and my numeric value is match duration in minutes.

B0 · My group, outcome and value

b_data <- sports %>%
  mutate(
    group = surface,
    has_outcome = minutes > 120,
    value = minutes
  )

b_data %>%
  count(group, has_outcome) %>%
  print(n = Inf)

   0.00   72.00   89.00   96.22  116.00  224.00     133 




B1 · The rate within each group

b1 <-  ggplot(b_data, aes(y = group, fill = has_outcome)) +
  geom_bar(position = "fill") +
  labs(x = "Share of the group", y = NULL, fill = "Match over 120 minutes")

show_plot(b1)







Figure 5: Share of each group with the outcome.





The plot shows that hard courts have the highest proportion of matches lasting more than 120 minutes, at approximately 24.3%. Grass follows at 19.1%, while clay has the lowest proportion at 17.0%. Shares are more useful than raw counts here because the three surfaces have different numbers of matches.


B2 · A mean with its two spreads

b2_summary <- b_data %>%
  drop_na(value) %>%
  group_by(group) %>%
  summarize(
    n = n(),
    mean = mean(value),
    sd = sd(value),
    se = sd / sqrt(n)
  )

b2_summary

# A tibble: 3 × 5
  group     n  mean    sd    se
  <chr> <int> <dbl> <dbl> <dbl>
1 Clay    503  96.3  32.9 1.47 
2 Grass   508  93.9  30.1 1.34 
3 Hard   1269  97.1  31.6 0.886

b2 <- ggplot(b2_summary,
             aes(x = mean, y = group,
                 xmin = mean - se,
                 xmax = mean + se)) +
  geom_pointrange() +
  # Many groups, and the labels touch the points? Keep every group, and use
  # vjust = -0.8, size = 3 instead of nudge_y = 0.3.
  geom_text(aes(label = paste("n =", n)), nudge_y = 0.3) +
  labs(x = "Mean match duration (minutes)", y = NULL)

show_plot(b2)







Figure 6: Mean in each group, with ± one standard error and group size.

The difference between hard and grass is larger than their standard errors but much smaller than their standard deviations, meaning individual match durations vary a lot even though the averages are fairly close.

The zoomed plot’s Lie Factor (largest vs smallest group) is 1.58.
The zoomed plot displays only the portion of the bars above 250, making the differences between the surfaces appear larger. The filtered plot is empty because “scale_x_continuous()” removes the bars when their starting point of zero falls outside the selected limits. The Lie Factor is approximately 1.58, meaning the zoomed graph exaggerates the visual difference by about 1.58 times. I would publish the original plot because it shows the full counts without exaggerating their differences. A narrow time window would also hide matches played outside the selected period compared with the full 2018–2022 dataset.


B4 · Each group’s share of everyone with the outcome

b4_shares <- b_data %>%
  filter(has_outcome) %>%
  count(group) %>%
  mutate(share = n / sum(n))

b4_shares

# A tibble: 3 × 3

  <chr> <int> <dbl>
1 Clay    108 0.210

  geom_col() +
  labs(x = "Share of every surface with the outcome", y = NULL)

show_plot(b4)







Figure 8: Each group’s share of everyone with the outcome.





B1 and B4 both show that hard courts have the highest representation of matches lasting over 120 minutes. However, B1 compares the rate within each surface, while B4 compares each surface’s share of all matches lasting over 120 minutes. Clay has a slightly larger share than grass in B4, even though grass has a higher within-surface rate in B1, because clay has more matches overall.
